passage.title: Echoes Under Etowah
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Near Cartersville, Georgia, six flat-topped earth mounds rise above the north bank of the Etowah River. Long ago, this valley was a thriving town where thousands of people lived, traded, and held grand games. Today, thick green grass covers the broad fields between the tall mounds. To a park guest walking the trail, the open lawn looks quite empty. Yet just a few feet under the turf lies the plan of an old town.

For many years, teams had only one way to check buried walls. They dug deep trenches with metal spades. Digging could find clay pots or stone tools, but it also sliced through delicate dirt floors that could never be fixed. Out of respect for native history and fragile soil layers, modern researchers needed a way to peer underground without turning a single spade of dirt. They turned to a tool called ground radar.

A radar cart looks much like a push mower rolled across the grass in straight, even rows. As the wheels roll forward, a small box sends safe radio waves down into the dirt. When those waves hit packed clay, post holes, or stone hearths, they bounce back to a screen on the cart. Buried council houses and wide clay plazas, hidden beneath centuries of grass and river silt, are clearly mapped by the radar team on a digital screen. Different soil densities show up as crisp dark lines.

At Etowah, these radar maps showed a busy town plan that no spade had ever found. Beneath the quiet lawn, the scans traced a vast central plaza where citizens once gathered for games and council meetings. Around the edge of that plaza stood rows of large wood halls, tall walls, and deep food pits. The builders had leveled and packed the red clay so tightly that it still reflects radio waves after nine hundred years.

Because ground radar leaves the earth intact, future guests will be able to see Etowah just as it stands today. Park rangers now use the maps to keep heavy mowers and new paths away from the most fragile buried walls. By blending modern tools with deep respect for the past, teams can read the story of an old Georgia town while keeping its sacred ground whole.

tier2Words.definition: easily damaged or broken if not handled with great care

tier2Words.definition: how tightly packed or solid different materials are
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root densus ('thick or closely packed')

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Buried council houses and wide clay plazas, hidden beneath centuries of grass and river silt, are clearly mapped by the radar team on a digital screen."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who performs the action of mapping, and what is being mapped?

options.text: Centuries of grass and river silt map the radar team onto a digital screen.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action backward! Grass and river silt are just the dirt layers covering the old town; the radar team is who maps the buried buildings.

options.text: Park guests draw maps of the Etowah River on clay tablets with metal spades.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 explains that modern teams stopped digging with metal spades, and park guests only walk the trail above the grass.

options.text: Buried council houses map the river silt using a push mower.
options.childFeedback: Buried council houses are underground ruins—they cannot push a radar cart or map the river silt!

options.text: The radar team maps the buried council houses and wide clay plazas.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by the radar team' right after 'are clearly mapped' shows that the radar team performs the mapping, and the buried council houses and wide clay plazas are what get mapped.

questions.provingSentenceText: Buried council houses and wide clay plazas, hidden beneath centuries of grass and river silt, are clearly mapped by the radar team on a digital screen.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by the radar team' right after 'are clearly mapped' shows that the radar team performs the mapping, and the buried council houses and wide clay plazas are what get mapped.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'Buried council houses and wide clay plazas' receive the action 'are clearly mapped,' while 'by the radar team' identifies the actor performing the mapping.
questions.retryHint: Look at the 'by' phrase right after 'are clearly mapped' in Paragraph 3 to see who does the mapping.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 5:

"Because ground radar leaves the earth intact, future guests will be able to see Etowah just as it stands today."

What does the word intact mean as it is used in Paragraph 5?

options.text: Dug up into deep open trenches across the lawn
options.childFeedback: Digging open trenches with spades is the old damaging method from Paragraph 2 that ground radar replaced so the earth stays 'intact.'

options.text: Paved over with modern concrete parking lots
options.childFeedback: Park rangers even keep heavy mowers and new paths away from fragile buried walls in Paragraph 5, so nothing is paved over with concrete.

options.text: Undamaged, whole, and left in its natural state
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, 'intact' means undamaged, whole, and left in its natural state, because ground radar lets scientists map buried walls without digging trenches and keeps the sacred ground whole.

options.text: Flooded by water from the nearby Etowah River
options.childFeedback: The mounds sit above the north bank of the Etowah River, and radar waves do not flood the grassy lawn with water.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because ground radar leaves the earth intact, future guests will be able to see Etowah just as it stands today.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 5, 'intact' means undamaged, whole, and left in its natural state, because ground radar lets scientists map buried walls without digging trenches and keeps the sacred ground whole.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 5 contrasts radar scanning with shovel digging and notes that the site remains 'just as it stands today' and 'whole,' proving that 'intact' means undisturbed and undamaged.
questions.retryHint: Look at the clues 'without turning a single spade of dirt' (Paragraph 2) and 'keeping its sacred ground whole' (Paragraph 5).

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 4, why does the ancient plaza floor at Etowah still bounce radio waves back to the surface today?

options.text: Park rangers buried sheets of shiny copper foil beneath the grass every spring.
options.childFeedback: Park rangers never bury copper foil at Etowah—digging into the lawn would damage the fragile soil layers they are trying to protect.

options.text: The ancient builders leveled and packed the red clay so tightly that it remains dense underground.
options.childFeedback: The last sentence of Paragraph 4 explains that the ancient builders leveled and packed the red clay of the plaza so tightly that it remains dense enough to reflect radio waves after nine hundred years.

options.text: The Etowah River freezes into solid ice underneath the six mounds all year long.
options.childFeedback: The Etowah River in Georgia never freezes into solid underground ice all year long; the radio waves bounce off packed clay, post holes, and stone hearths.

options.text: Radio waves only bounce off loose green grass blades on top of the lawn.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that the radio waves travel down into the dirt and bounce off packed clay, post holes, and stone hearths beneath centuries of grass.

questions.provingSentenceText: The builders had leveled and packed the red clay so tightly that it still reflects radio waves after nine hundred years.
questions.childTip: The last sentence of Paragraph 4 explains that the ancient builders leveled and packed the red clay of the plaza so tightly that it remains dense enough to reflect radio waves after nine hundred years.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explicitly states that the ancient builders leveled and packed the red clay so tightly that it still reflects radio waves nine hundred years later.
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 4 to see what the ancient builders did to the red clay.

questions.prompt: How does the author organize Paragraph 2 to show why researchers adopted ground radar?

options.text: By explaining the problem of how spade digging damaged fragile soil layers and introducing radar as the solution
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 uses a problem-and-solution structure: it explains that digging trenches with metal spades sliced through delicate dirt floors that could never be fixed, and then shows how researchers turned to ground radar to peer underground without digging.

options.text: By listing the names and ages of every scientist who has worked near Cartersville
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 never lists the personal names or ages of individual scientists.

options.text: By comparing the height of the Etowah mounds to modern skyscrapers in Atlanta
options.childFeedback: Neither Paragraph 2 nor the rest of the passage compares the Etowah earth mounds to Atlanta skyscrapers.

options.text: By arguing that clay pots and stone tools have no value to historians
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 notes that digging could find clay pots or stone tools, but researchers wanted to stop slicing through fragile dirt floors—not because pots and tools had no value.

questions.provingSentenceText: Out of respect for native history and fragile soil layers, modern researchers needed a way to peer underground without turning a single spade of dirt.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 uses a problem-and-solution structure: it explains that digging trenches with metal spades sliced through delicate dirt floors that could never be fixed, and then shows how researchers turned to ground radar to peer underground without digging.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 uses a problem-and-solution structure: digging trenches sliced through delicate floors (problem), so researchers turned to ground radar to look underground without digging (solution).
questions.retryHint: Compare the problem with metal spades in the first half of Paragraph 2 with the new tool introduced at the end of Paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which inference about the flat grassy fields between the mounds at Etowah is best supported by the passage?

options.text: The fields between the mounds were never used by the ancient residents because the soil was too soft.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 shows the exact opposite: ancient builders packed the red clay tightly to make a vast central plaza where citizens gathered for games and council meetings.

options.text: Although the fields look empty from above, they hold the buried layout of an organized town center.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 1 and 4 show that although the grassy fields between the mounds look empty from above today, radar scans revealed a vast buried central plaza surrounded by wood halls, walls, and food pits.

options.text: All ancient buildings at Etowah were built on rafts floating in the middle of the river.
options.childFeedback: The town sat on the land above the north bank of the Etowah River, with post holes and clay plazas in the soil—not on floating river rafts.

options.text: Park rangers must dig up the entire central plaza every winter to protect it from frost.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 2 and 5 emphasize that researchers and rangers leave the earth untouched and never dig up the central plaza.

questions.provingSentenceText: Beneath the quiet lawn, the scans traced a vast central plaza where citizens once gathered for games and council meetings.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 1 and 4 show that although the grassy fields between the mounds look empty from above today, radar scans revealed a vast buried central plaza surrounded by wood halls, walls, and food pits.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 1 and 4 show that while the grassy fields between the mounds appear empty to a casual walker, radar scans beneath the lawn revealed a vast central plaza surrounded by council buildings and walls.
questions.retryHint: Compare how the grassy lawn looks to a park guest in Paragraph 1 with what the radar scans found under that lawn in Paragraph 4.
